opus-5.5.text:
I think it matters enormously, and I'd go so far as to say it's one of the central questions we have to get right.

Let me start with an observation from biology and child development. If you look at the evolutionary timeline, vision, locomotion, and manipulation have been around for hundreds of millions of years. Language is a very recent arrival, maybe a few hundred thousand years at most. So language sits on top of an enormous foundation of perceptual and motor competence. It didn't evolve in a vacuum. It evolved in creatures that already understood objects, space, causality, other agents, and how to act in the world.

The same holds for children. Before a child says their first words, they've already spent a year looking at things, grasping things, dropping things, crawling around. When a child learns the word "cup," they're attaching a label to something they already know a great deal about: how it looks from different angles, that it holds liquid, that it falls if you let go, that you can drink from it. The word is a pointer into a rich, grounded representation.

Now, with large language models we've done something historically unusual. We've built systems that learn from language alone, at a scale no human ever experiences, and they're remarkably capable. I don't want to dismiss that; it's a genuine achievement. But I think these models are, in a sense, learning the shadow of the world rather than the world itself. Text is what people wrote down, and people don't bother writing down the things everyone knows from physical experience. Nobody writes "if I push the glass off the table, it falls and may break" because every three-year-old knows it. So there are gaps in what you can learn from text, and those gaps are precisely the commonsense physical and spatial understanding that's foundational.

So my view is that the path to more robust intelligence runs through embodiment and perception. You want systems that learn from vision, from touch, from acting and seeing consequences, and then language gets layered on top and connected to those representations. That's when words acquire meaning in the deeper sense, rather than just statistical association with other words.

There's also a practical side. If we want robots that operate in homes, hospitals, or factories, they need to understand the physical world as it is, not as it's described. Language can be a wonderful interface, letting you tell a robot "put the dishes away," but executing that requires grounded perception and control. I think the most exciting work right now combines these: the broad knowledge from language models with the grounded learning that comes from sensorimotor experience. Neither alone is sufficient. Together, I think they can get us much closer to the kind of general intelligence we see in humans and animals.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it matters enormously, and my view on this comes from thinking about how intelligence actually arose. If you look at evolution, the brain wasn't built to do language or mathematics. It was built to help an animal move around, find food, avoid predators, and manipulate objects in the world. Perception and action came first, and they've been refined over hundreds of millions of years. Language, by comparison, is a very recent arrival, maybe on the order of a hundred thousand years. So in the natural order of things, language sits on top of a huge foundation of sensorimotor intelligence.

Now, in AI we've done things somewhat backwards. The big successes recently have come from language models trained on enormous amounts of text, and they're remarkable. But text is a description of the world written by people who already understood the world through their bodies and their senses. When a child learns the word "heavy" or "fragile" or "slippery," that word is attaching to something the child has already experienced by lifting things and dropping things. The model only gets the shadow of that experience, the verbal residue. It can be surprisingly good at manipulating those shadows, but there are limits to how far you can go without the thing itself.

This is why I think robotics and embodied learning are so important, not just as an application area but for the science of intelligence. An agent that acts in the world gets something text can never give you: it gets to test its beliefs. You predict what will happen when you push the cup, you push it, and the world tells you whether you were right. That closed loop between prediction and consequence is, to me, the core of what it means to understand something. It's also where common sense comes from. The physical intuitions we all have about objects, space, and causality are learned by every infant long before they can speak, and they're learned by interacting, not by being told.

I'd add one more point, which is about efficiency. Children learn with astonishingly little data compared to our models. A two-year-old has heard a few million words, not trillions of tokens. I suspect part of the reason is that their learning is grounded. The visual and physical experience provides structure that makes language learning much easier, because the concepts are already partly there waiting for names. So I'm not saying language doesn't matter. It obviously does, it's how we transmit knowledge across generations. But I believe the next real advances in intelligence will come from systems that connect language to perception and action, so that words mean something because they're tied to what the system has actually seen and done.

astra-6.text:
I think it matters a great deal. Language lets us talk about the world, but the words themselves are not the world. Take a word like “push.” A child comes to understand pushing by acting on objects, seeing them move, feeling resistance, and discovering that some things are harder to move than others. The word becomes attached to that collection of experiences.

Now, language is extraordinarily useful because it allows us to learn from other people without having to experience everything ourselves. But somebody has to have that experience. If I explain something to you, I’m relying on concepts that you already understand, and many of those concepts ultimately come from perception and action.

So I think the interesting challenge is to bring these capabilities together: seeing, acting, and communicating. An intelligent system should be able to connect a description to what it observes, use that description to guide an action, and learn from what actually happens. That connection gives language meaning beyond its relationships to other words.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it matters a great deal. Language lets us communicate about the world, but the meaning of those words ultimately has to connect to perception and action. Take a simple instruction like, “Pick up the cup.” You have to recognize the cup, understand where it is, and know how to grasp it. The sentence itself doesn’t give you all of that knowledge.

A child learns these things through experience—looking, touching, moving, and seeing what happens. And that experience provides a foundation for understanding language. You learn that objects can fall, that some things are heavy, that pushing something has consequences.

Now, you can certainly learn a tremendous amount from language. We do that ourselves. But language is a compressed description of the world; it leaves many things unsaid because we assume a shared understanding. For an intelligent system, the challenge is to connect those descriptions to the world they describe. That’s why I think perception, action, and language need to be studied together.
